title: Iran and US keep negotiating over ceasefire, fighting drags on
lead: Iran and the US are haggling over a proposal for a ceasefire. It is yet another attempt to end the war that began at the end of February with an Israeli-American air offensive against Iran. The weapons are more or less silent at the moment, but a test of strength is still under way between the US and Iran in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran demands control over the economically crucial strait, while America tries to enforce a blockade of Iranian ships. Neither can fully get its way. Iran turns out to be less able to hold the world economy in a stranglehold than initially feared. But that does not simply mean the struggle will be decided in America's favor. Leverage Tehran says the Strait of Hormuz remains closed to ships that do not coordinate their passage with the Iranian authorities. Several ships that did not comply have been attacked by Iran in recent days, reports the elite corps Islamic Revolutionary Guard. Three oil tankers in the strait were hit by projectiles on Tuesday, says maritime intelligence agency Marisks. It is unclear whether these are the same ships Iran is said to have attacked, but the psychological effect is no less for it. The crews of tankers in the Persian Gulf may be discouraged from continuing. Since August the US has been trying to force a breakthrough. The American navy quietly escorts oil tankers through the strait every day. As a result of this operation, more oil now reaches the world market via the Strait of Hormuz. If that trend continues and oil exports reach the pre-war level, Iran risks losing its grip on its biggest trump card: the high oil price as leverage against Washington. Declaration of intent Perhaps because of this strategic setback, Tehran is trying to revive a previously signed declaration of intent between the two countries. In June the US and Iran agreed to lay down their arms, open the Strait of Hormuz and reach a permanent peace agreement through negotiations within two months. But Iran and the US soon began attacking each other again, and this declaration of intent was, in the words of President Trump, "over". Last week Iran presented a new, "improved" version of it to Qatari mediators and said normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could resume under conditions. President Trump rejected that new version of the declaration of intent, but the mediation continues. The text drawn up by Iran has not been made public, but based on leaked details, analysts do not think Iran is proposing anything substantially different from last time. The American think tank Institute for the Study of War points out that Iran maintains its position that it has the right to control traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Hardliners Iran's economy is in decline. Oil revenues are suffering badly from the American blockade. The Iranian rial, the national currency, has collapsed and there is a severe shortage of hard currency. Inflation has been above 80 percent for months. Although some Iranian leaders are worried about a popular uprising like the one earlier this year, the regime does not seem inclined to give in to American demands in exchange for lifting the sanctions. Supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not appeared in public since taking office. In his absence, it is the hardliners of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard who have the most influence in Tehran. They seem far from ready to give up the familiar goals: exercising control over the Strait of Hormuz, continuing the Iranian nuclear program and continuing to support militant allies abroad such as Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen. Every one of them is a goal the Americans are fiercely opposed to.

title: EU ministers want even stricter migration policy for emergencies at the border
lead: The ink on the EU migration pact has barely dried, and yet work is already under way on new measures to get even more of a grip on migration to the European Union. During a meeting in Luxembourg, almost all European asylum ministers argue for extra options to prevent a situation like the one in Ceuta this summer. Emergency measures Hopes rest, among other things, on an announced package of measures for emergencies and on an expansion of the mandate of the European border agency Frontex. "The events of this summer make clear that we must have more options," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen during her annual speech to the European Parliament. A frequently mentioned option as a crisis measure is to temporarily relieve countries of the obligation to process an asylum application in the event of a sudden mass influx. 'Unique situations' Migration Minister Van den Brink thinks it is a good idea. "I think that is the only way to deal with this. Because such a large group of people crossing a border, in fact storming a border, simply means a breach of the border. You have to repair it immediately by putting that group straight back." Van den Brink does not object to people thus no longer getting a chance to apply for asylum. "These are truly unique situations. For those unique moments when that happens, you need something in your toolbox to be able to respond." Now it is a matter of waiting for a concrete crisis proposal from the European Commission. Only when that arrives will it become clear whether this idea makes it to the finish line. It will also be discussed with the heads of government of the EU member states at the next EU summit. In a few weeks the European Commission will also come with a proposal to give the Frontex border guards more options. The Commission has wanted more staff at the agency for some time and now also wants to give it a role in deporting migrants to countries outside the EU. Frontex should also start monitoring social media for signs of new crisis situations at the EU's external border. Success? Meanwhile, the European Commission leaves no opportunity unused to stress that the migration pact that entered into force last June is a success. The main evidence cited is the sharp drop in asylum figures, even though that drop had already begun before the pact took effect. That the statistics do not tell the whole story anyway was proven by the situation in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. The number of migrants who arrived there within a few days exceeded anything the EU had prepared for, but is seen as an exception. Even so, the situation made clear that solidarity among EU member states on asylum policy is anything but a given. That, while the migration pact is supposed to ensure, besides a better asylum procedure, more solidarity among members. The asylum ministers received an oral explanation today on how the Migration Pact is going, but an official report, which the Commission had earlier promised for the coming EU summit, has been postponed and will probably come shortly after it. It shows that the European Commission wants to prevent countries from finding a reason to start pointing fingers at each other again, as right after Ceuta. Return hubs Ahead of the EU asylum meeting, the Netherlands also held a separate meeting with Austria, Germany, Greece and Denmark. This so-called 'leading group' of EU countries has the ambition to set up deportation centers outside the European Union as soon as possible and has met several times over the past year. title: Co-pilot was radicalised, says Netanyahu, many questions still open
lead: Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu said in an interview with Fox News that the co-pilot of the Flydubai aircraft is a radicalised Muslim. He is said to have been indoctrinated with Islamist ideas and to have been suicidal. What kind of past the man has exactly is not yet clear. Netanyahu said he had no specific information about that. Many other questions also remain open for now. These are images made in the aircraft yesterday. The footage is intense: Staying with the co-pilot: he has Omani nationality and that raises questions. Israel has no diplomatic relations with that country, and so the pilot presumably should never have been on the flight. Israeli Transport Minister Miri Regev points out that the agreement with the UAE is that only pilots holding a passport from countries with which Israel maintains diplomatic relations should have been on the flight. Regev now wants to know whether Flydubai has broken the aviation agreement. Pilots are also checked One possibility is that the co-pilot held two passports. But according to experts that chance seems small because it is exceptional in Oman. Another question is whether the co-pilot really had a knife on him. That should not be possible. Pilots, like passengers, are extensively checked at an airport. The rules are more or less the same. A knife should never have been allowed on board. Or did he strike with an axe? One is always on board for emergencies, so that a panel can still be broken open in the event of very serious problems. Or a door. Even so, a witness saw the co-pilot with a knife in his hand. Investigation in several countries More answers may take a while, because the investigation into the near-crash is complex. That is because it is taking place in several locations and the diplomatic relations between the countries involved are precarious. In Israel itself, security services are investigating the incident. For example, all passengers were questioned by the secret service Mossad on their return to Israel, the BBC describes. Because the aircraft flew under the flag of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), of which Dubai is part, that country is leading the investigation. The co-pilot has meanwhile been handed over to the United Arab Emirates, says Saudi Arabia. He was treated for his injuries in Saudi Arabia today because the aircraft made an emergency landing in that country. According to media reports, Saudi Arabia has already questioned him. The UAE's chief prosecutor confirms that an investigation has been started and that it is also looking at whether terrorism is involved. Prime Minister Netanyahu already drew a comparison with the 9/11 attacks in the US, although he added that much still has to be investigated. A hero There seems to be less and less doubt about the role of the other pilot. The Indian Smit Machchhar seems to have played a key role in preventing a fatal crash of the aircraft. Although already injured, he managed to open the heavily secured cockpit door so that passengers could overpower the co-pilot and get the aircraft back onto a level path. He is now being praised as a hero, first of all by the prime minister of India. He described his actions on X : "Captain Smit Machchhar has shown the world the highest form of courage." The Embassy of India in the UAE says on X that he is recovering well after his operation. Israel on alert Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu also praises Machchhar: "Although he had been stabbed and seriously wounded, he resisted, opened the cockpit door and made it possible for passengers and crew members to overpower the attacker. In this way a disaster in the air was prevented." The incident comes at a time when the Israeli services are preparing for the elections, the first since the terror attacks of 7 October 2023. That day also brings extra alertness. Meanwhile, Israeli media report that the head of the domestic security service Shin Bet has been worried for some time about flights from the Emirates. Security is said to have been insufficient. But against that stands Netanyahu's statement. He says there were no concrete signals that the incident was coming.

title: Fifteen bodies found in Himalaya base camp after Sunday's avalanche
lead: Emergency services in Nepal have recovered fifteen bodies of mountaineers who were buried by an avalanche on Sunday. They were found in the base camp of the mountain Himlung Himal, close to the border with Tibet. One climber is still missing. The group was setting up the base camp on the mountain, which is more than 7,000 metres high. They were putting up tents and fixing ropes for the climbing season, which is now beginning. Most were mountain guides, but there were also cooks. On Sunday the bodies of two mountain guides were found quickly. Over the past days rescue teams have searched for the others, at first still hoping to find survivors. But over the past days only dead were found. Today eight more bodies were pulled out from under the deep snow, bringing the death toll to fifteen. The missing person is still being searched for, but according to the director of the Nepalese mountaineering organisation the chance of finding them is small, and the recovery operation may soon be ended. Severe weather from cyclone Nepal and India were hit on Sunday by severe weather caused by a cyclone over the Bay of Bengal. For days there was heavy rain and snow. Rivers burst their banks and there were landslides. Dozens died: 31 in Nepal and 80 in India. The avalanche that the climbers were caught in was also a result of the severe weather. Nepal was and still is busy recovering from the previous disaster. In August an ice avalanche left a trail of destruction. More than 1,450 people died and thousands of people are still missing. Emergency aid routes blocked The severe weather of last weekend has also caused roads and bridges to be blocked. Some routes were closed by the government as a precaution. As a result, all kinds of places are still barely accessible for emergency aid. Climbing is one of the most important sources of income for Nepal. Eight of the fourteen highest mountains in the world are located in the country. A permit is needed to climb a mountain such as Himlung Himal. For this season some 600 permits have been issued to climbers from almost 70 countries.
